lines.text: Before electric refrigerators were invented in the nineteen-twenties, how did families keep their milk and meat from spoiling?
Every household relied on a wooden cabinet lined with tin or zinc, called an icebox.
During freezing winters, commercial ice harvesters sawed millions of tons of natural ice blocks from frozen northern lakes.
The giant blocks were packed in sawdust insulation and stored in massive icehouses until hot summer months.
Every week, the local iceman delivered twenty-five pound ice blocks with iron tongs straight into home kitchens.
Families placed the melting ice in the top compartment, allowing dense cold air to sink over meat and butter.
Electric refrigeration transformed global nutrition, food safety, and modern civilization forever.
